results.name: rule_consistent_inside_minus_outside_range
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share a last digit or are all multiples of some m in 3..12, for non-example targets that satisfy that same rule, yes-rate when the target lies inside the examples' [min,max] minus when it lies outside; observed above model means people restrict an arithmetic rule to the examples' magnitude range (rule-within-range) more than the model's rule hypotheses (which ignore range) allow, below means less.
results.code:
# name: rule_consistent_inside_minus_outside_range
# description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share a last digit or are all multiples of some m in 3..12, for non-example targets that satisfy that same rule, yes-rate when the target lies inside the examples' [min,max] minus when it lies outside; observed above model means people restrict an arithmetic rule to the examples' magnitude range (rule-within-range) more than the model's rule hypotheses (which ignore range) allow, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True)
    ex = parts.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n_ex = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    exz = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=0.0)
    present = ~np.isnan(ex)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    consistent = np.zeros(len(df), dtype=bool)
    ld = exz % 10
    same_ld = np.all(~present | (ld == ld[:, [0]]), axis=1)
    consistent |= same_ld & (t % 10 == ld[:, 0])
    for m in range(3, 13):
        allm = np.all(~present | (exz % m == 0), axis=1)
        consistent |= allm & (t % m == 0)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1), np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    base = (n_ex >= 2) & consistent & ~is_ex
    inside = base & (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    outside = base & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    if inside.sum() == 0 or outside.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[inside].mean() - r[outside].mean())

results.name: within_set_target_spread
results.description: Mean, over example sets asked about with >= 8 distinct targets, of the variance across that set's targets of the per-(set,target) yes-rate; observed above model means people differentiate targets within a set more sharply than the model's (too flat) posterior-predictive probabilities, below means the model differentiates targets more than people do.

results.name: even_rule_violator_yes_rate
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples are all multiples of some m in {4,6,8,12} (largest such m used), the yes-rate for non-example EVEN targets that are not multiples of m (e.g. 22 or 82 after "20,32,92"); observed below model means people reject parity-consistent numbers that break the specific multiples rule more firmly than the model (whose broad "even"/interval hypotheses leak probability to them), above means they accept them more.
results.code:
# name: even_rule_violator_yes_rate
# description: Among multi-example sets whose examples are all multiples of some m in {4,6,8,12} (largest such m used), the yes-rate for non-example EVEN targets that are not multiples of m (e.g. 22 or 82 after "20,32,92"); observed below model means people reject parity-consistent numbers that break the specific multiples rule more firmly than the model (whose broad "even"/interval hypotheses leak probability to them), above means they accept them more.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True)
    ex = parts.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n_ex = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    m_chosen = np.zeros(len(df), dtype=int)
    for m in [4, 6, 8, 12]:
        allm = np.all(np.isnan(ex) | (np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=0.0) % m == 0), axis=1)
        m_chosen = np.where(allm, m, m_chosen)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    safe_m = np.where(m_chosen > 0, m_chosen, 1)
    mask = (n_ex >= 2) & (m_chosen > 0) & (t % 2 == 0) & (t % safe_m != 0) & ~is_ex
    if mask.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[mask].mean())

results.name: participant_set_interpretation_spread
results.description: Mean, over example sets with >= 8 distinct targets, of the variance across participants (blocks delimited by trial_index resets) of each participant's yes-rate on that set; observed above model means individuals each adopt a different hypothesis for a set (broad vs narrow, hypothesis sampling) rather than all responding from one shared averaged posterior, below means people are more uniform than independent Bernoulli responding implies.
results.code:
# name: participant_set_interpretation_spread
# description: Mean, over example sets with >= 8 distinct targets, of the variance across participants (blocks delimited by trial_index resets) of each participant's yes-rate on that set; observed above model means individuals each adopt a different hypothesis for a set (broad vs narrow, hypothesis sampling) rather than all responding from one shared averaged posterior, below means people are more uniform than independent Bernoulli responding implies.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    pid = np.cumsum(np.r_[True, np.diff(ti) < 0])
    d = pd.DataFrame({"s": df["number_set"].astype(str).to_numpy(), "t": df["target"].to_numpy(),
                      "p": pid, "r": df["rating"].to_numpy()})
    nt = d.groupby("s")["t"].nunique()
    keep = nt[nt >= 8].index
    d = d[d["s"].isin(keep)]
    if len(d) == 0:
        return 0.0
    ps = d.groupby(["s", "p"])["r"].mean().reset_index()
    v = ps.groupby("s")["r"].var(ddof=0)
    return float(v.mean())

results.name: above_minus_below_range_yes_rate
results.description: For non-example targets outside the examples' [min,max] and within 15 of the nearest range edge, yes-rate for targets above the max minus targets below the min; the model's intervals extend symmetrically, so observed above model means people extrapolate upward (to larger numbers) more than downward, below means downward more.
results.code:
# name: above_minus_below_range_yes_rate
# description: For non-example targets outside the examples' [min,max] and within 15 of the nearest range edge, yes-rate for targets above the max minus targets below the min; the model's intervals extend symmetrically, so observed above model means people extrapolate upward (to larger numbers) more than downward, below means downward more.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True)
    ex = parts.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1), np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    above = (t > hi) & (t - hi <= 15)
    below = (t < lo) & (lo - t <= 15)
    if above.sum() == 0 or below.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[above].mean() - r[below].mean())

results.name: two_example_common_divisor_yes_rate
results.description: Among 2-example sets whose examples share a common divisor >= 3 (or a last digit), the yes-rate for non-example targets that also share that divisor (gcd(gcd of examples, target) >= 3) or that last digit; observed above model means people commit to the specific arithmetic rule from just two examples more sharply than the model's size principle + interval competition predicts, below means less.
results.code:
# name: two_example_common_divisor_yes_rate
# description: Among 2-example sets whose examples share a common divisor >= 3 (or a last digit), the yes-rate for non-example targets that also share that divisor (gcd(gcd of examples, target) >= 3) or that last digit; observed above model means people commit to the specific arithmetic rule from just two examples more sharply than the model's size principle + interval competition predicts, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True)
    n_ex = parts.notna().sum(axis=1)
    two = (n_ex == 2).to_numpy()
    a = pd.to_numeric(parts[0], errors="coerce").fillna(1).astype(int).to_numpy()
    b = pd.to_numeric(parts[1], errors="coerce").fillna(1).astype(int).to_numpy() if parts.shape[1] > 1 else a
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    g = np.gcd(a, b)
    shared_div = np.gcd(g, t) >= 3
    same_ld = (a % 10 == b % 10) & (t % 10 == a % 10)
    eligible = two & ((g >= 3) | (a % 10 == b % 10)) & (t != a) & (t != b)
    mask = eligible & (shared_div | same_ld)
    if mask.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[mask].mean())

results.name: ruleless_set_inrange_yes_rate
results.description: Among multi-example sets with no shared arithmetic structure (examples not all the same parity, not sharing a last digit, gcd < 3), the yes-rate for non-example targets strictly inside the examples' [min,max]; observed above model means people fill in the magnitude range of structureless examples more than the model's Erlang interval prior predicts, below means less.
results.code:
# name: ruleless_set_inrange_yes_rate
# description: Among multi-example sets with no shared arithmetic structure (examples not all the same parity, not sharing a last digit, gcd < 3), the yes-rate for non-example targets strictly inside the examples' [min,max]; observed above model means people fill in the magnitude range of structureless examples more than the model's Erlang interval prior predicts, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True)
    ex = parts.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    present = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n_ex = present.sum(axis=1)
    exi = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=0.0).astype(int)
    g = np.gcd.reduce(np.where(present, exi, 0), axis=1)
    par = exi % 2
    same_par = np.all(~present | (par == par[:, [0]]), axis=1)
    ld = exi % 10
    same_ld = np.all(~present | (ld == ld[:, [0]]), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1), np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    mask = (n_ex >= 2) & ~same_par & ~same_ld & (g < 3) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~is_ex
    if mask.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[mask].mean())

results.name: single_example_last_digit_match
results.description: Among sets whose examples do NOT all share a last digit, for non-example targets more than 5 away from every example, yes-rate for targets ending in the same digit as at least one example minus yes-rate for targets ending in no example's digit; observed above model means people generalise from partial surface similarity to single examples (last digit) beyond what the model's whole-set-consistent rules allow, below means less.
results.code:
# name: single_example_last_digit_match
# description: Among sets whose examples do NOT all share a last digit, for non-example targets more than 5 away from every example, yes-rate for targets ending in the same digit as at least one example minus yes-rate for targets ending in no example's digit; observed above model means people generalise from partial surface similarity to single examples (last digit) beyond what the model's whole-set-consistent rules allow, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True)
    ex = parts.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    ld = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, ex % 10)
    first = ld[:, 0]
    all_same = np.all(np.isnan(ld) | (ld == first[:, None]), axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    match = np.any(ld == (t % 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    base = (~all_same) & (dist > 5)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    a, b = base & match, base & ~match
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
